channel: Oil volumes and prices (conditional on security)
direction: Positive if flows normalise (volume-led); Negative if disruption persists
quantified: Illustrative, our assumptions, not a forecast. Saudi crude supply averaged 7.9 mb/d in Jan–Sep 2026 (final Budget Statement). Returning to the October level of 9.19 mb/d (OPEC secondary sources) would be about +16%; reaching the 10.48 mb/d OPEC+ required level, about +33%. If Brent falls from about USD 96 (Jan–Oct 2026 average) to EIA's 2027 forecast of USD 85.8 (about −11%), crude export revenue would change by roughly +3% to +18%.
rationale: The final budget's growth path assumes oil output recovers: real GDP +10.9% in 2027 after −2.1% in 2026, with oil activity −14.6% through Q3 2026. A recovery is unlikely to reverse the 2026 price and volume effects symmetrically. The volume upside to the required level is larger than the likely price fall, so a normalisation case is net positive for sector revenue. If the escalation since 30 Sep 2026 persists (tankers hit in Hormuz on 21 and 25 Nov), volumes stay constrained instead. Output series quoted on one basis: OPEC secondary sources, 6.82 mb/d in Q2 and 9.19 mb/d in Oct 2026 (secondary, not read in the MOMR).
depends_on_execution: Hormuz and Red Sea security; OPEC+ 2027 levels (29 Nov 2026)
indicators_to_watch: Monthly Saudi output (one series); Brent; OPEC+ decision; Hormuz traffic

channel: Volumes, prices and export capacity
quantified: Historical context (not a policy effect): 9M 2026 realised crude +29.2% and liquids −15.2% (fact 2222-9M2026-REV). The budget gives no 2027 oil-revenue assumption.
rationale: Aramco carries almost all of the sector's oil price and volume exposure. A plan to raise East-West Pipeline throughput to about 10 mb/d is under consideration, with preliminary engineering and no final investment decision. If built, it would cut reliance on Hormuz but add capex. Its revenue effect is not determinable.
depends_on_execution: EWP expansion is under consideration (no FID); 2027 oil revenue not published
indicators_to_watch: Aramco FY2026 results; EWP FID

channel: Government funding needs, dividends, PIF and share sales
quantified: Historical context: Aramco's 2025 distributions of SAR 320.4bn equalled its free cash flow (company-reported; matches fact 2222-FY2025-FCF).
rationale: The deficit (SAR 190.6bn) and financing costs (+31.1% to SAR 93bn) keep the state and PIF reliant on Aramco's base dividend, which has recently risen 3.5% a year. The Minister's move to a National Privatization Strategy (about 202 projects) keeps government share sales open as a financing option; the last Aramco offering was in Jun 2024. Aramco's purchase of 49% of HUMAIN from PIF (SAR 9.9bn, Nov 2026) shows capital moving between PIF and Aramco. No change to Aramco's dividend or any share sale has been announced.
risks: Payout pressure alongside USD 50–55bn capex; share-sale overhang
indicators_to_watch: Aramco dividend declarations; privatisation announcements

channel: Domestic energy prices and subsidies
direction: Neutral / not determinable until the Jan 2027 price notices
quantified: Not quantified. Total subsidies fall 61.6% (SAR 48bn to 18bn), mainly support to electricity and water companies.
rationale: The budget changes electricity and water tariffs only. Aramco's regulated fuel and feedstock prices are set separately, and no 2027 change is confirmed. Any increase would raise Aramco's domestic revenue but reduce its price-equalisation income from the government. The budget does not say whether lower utility subsidies change the fuel prices charged to the power sector.
indicators_to_watch: Annual price notices; other income related to sales

channel: Freight rates, Aramco volumes and security
direction: Negative vs 2026 peak if flows normalise
quantified: Historical context: Bahri 9M 2026 revenue SAR 26.1bn vs 7.1bn (facts 4030-9M2026-REV, 4030-9M2025-REV); VLCC rates above USD 1m/day in Sep 2026.
rationale: Bahri's 2026 surge came from crisis freight rates and Aramco's rerouted exports. Normalisation would bring more cargo but lower rates, and rates would dominate. The government marine-insurance pool is described as cutting insurance costs on shipments arriving at Saudi ports. There is no evidence that it covers Bahri's export tankers, so it is not counted as support here. Security risk is company-specific: the Houthi blockade of Saudi shipping, the attack on the tanker AMZAN, and tankers hit in Nov 2026.
indicators_to_watch: VLCC TCE rates; Bahri Q4 2026; Red Sea and Hormuz incidents

channel: Refining margins, feedstock prices, Zakat and shareholder support
quantified: Historical context: Petro Rabigh 9M 2026 net profit SAR 6.7bn vs a SAR 3.3bn loss (facts 2380-9M2026-NI_ATTR, 2380-9M2025-NI_ATTR). Tariff effect not quantified.
rationale: The 2026 profit came from crisis refining margins, which are not a budget item and are likely to narrow as supply normalises. Feedstock price notices (each January) and Zakat on a now-profitable base are more direct cost channels than the electricity tariff. Petro Rabigh's own utility supply arrangements have not been verified. Aramco, with about 60%, remains the funding backstop.
indicators_to_watch: Product cracks; Petro Rabigh Q4 2026

channel: Upstream activity, geographic mix and acquisition debt
quantified: Historical context: 9M 2026 finance costs SAR 976m vs 668m, driven by borrowings that rose to about SAR 20bn after the Shelf Drilling acquisition, not by policy rates.
rationale: Restored Saudi output and the gas programme support rig demand. Maximum sustainable capacity is held at 12 mb/d, which limits new oil-capacity drilling. ADES differs from Arabian Drilling because it is now diversified beyond Saudi Arabia through Shelf, so it is less exposed to Saudi suspensions but carries more acquisition debt. Its Saudi segment fell 12.8% in 9M 2026. The rate channel is minor next to its own leverage.
indicators_to_watch: Aramco rig resumptions; ADES backlog

channel: Rig activity and refinancing
quantified: Not quantified. SAR 2bn sukuk due 3 Feb 2027; covenant waiver to 31 Mar 2027 (company filings).
rationale: Arabian Drilling received notices in Aug 2026 to resume all remaining suspended offshore rigs and expected full offshore utilisation by end-Q3 2026, so activity is recovering. The main risk is company-specific refinancing of the Feb 2027 sukuk in tighter funding conditions. Its link to government borrowing is indirect (Low confidence).
indicators_to_watch: Refinancing announcement; rig utilisation

channel: Equity-market exposure
quantified: Not quantified.
rationale: SARCO's results depend on dividends and its listed-share portfolio. It has no direct budget channel.
indicators_to_watch: TASI

channel: Corporate tax: Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (from 1 Jan 2027)
quantified: Not quantified: executive regulations pending.
rationale: A 15% minimum effective tax applies to constituent entities of groups with revenue of at least EUR 750m. In scope are likely Aramco (whose Saudi income already bears income tax), ADES (multi-country) and Bahri (if over the threshold). The effect depends on current effective tax rates by entity and on the regulations. No Zakat rule change for 2027 was found (search to 26 Nov 2026).
risks: Higher effective tax for low-taxed entities
indicators_to_watch: ZATCA regulations

channel: Government borrowing, deposits and bank liquidity
quantified: Gross domestic borrowing in 9M 2026 was SAR 235bn, about 7.7% of bank deposits (SAR 3,076bn); net of domestic repayments it was about SAR 193bn (6.3%). How much banks absorbed is not disclosed. 2027 net borrowing need: debt +SAR 190bn vs +SAR 214bn estimated for 2026.
rationale: The final Budget Statement states an intention for 2027 borrowing to 'focus on domestic and private market channels'; the size and mix await the NDMC 2027 plan. The 2027 need is smaller than 2026's. Funding is already tight: Fitch reports tighter and more expensive funding, and government-entity deposits at SAMA near a five-year low (about SAR 370bn on Fitch's measure; the budget's 'government reserves at SAMA' of SAR 399bn is a different measure). Time deposits now exceed demand deposits. On the simple ratio, loans exceed deposits (107% at 30 Sep 2026), but SAMA's regulatory ratio is below 85% at all ten banks against a 90% cap. That means wholesale-funding reliance rather than a binding limit. J.P. Morgan index inclusion of SAR sukuk from 29 Jan 2027 should add foreign demand.
indicators_to_watch: NDMC plan; SAR sukuk auctions; 3M SAIBOR; time-deposit share

channel: Government spending, projects, PIF and utilities lending
direction: Neutral to slightly negative vs the 2022–25 trend
quantified: Loan growth was 12.3% a year in 2022–25, then +6.4% y/y for listed-bank loans to Sep 2026. Fitch expects about 8% sector credit growth in 2027.
rationale: 2027 spending is 3% below the 2026 estimated outturn, but 6% above the FY2026 budget, and capex is 10% above the FY2026 budget. The Ministry of Finance attributes the −2.1% capex change mainly to military spending brought forward into 2026, not to civil project cuts. Project rescheduling is a stated signal without a list. Two further channels: PIF and government-related entities are large bank borrowers, so their project choices reach banks directly. Lower utility subsidies change the cash needs of the power and water companies, a fast-growing bank exposure. Loan growth should stay well below the 2022–25 pace, but roughly flat to slightly higher than in 2026.
indicators_to_watch: Quarterly budget capex; credit growth by sector

channel: Contractor payments
quantified: Not quantified.
rationale: The amended Government Tenders and Procurement Law bars a government entity from awarding new contracts if it has not addressed outstanding payments, as set out in the Implementing Regulations. If enforced, it should reduce payment delays to contractors, a recurring source of corporate credit stress.
indicators_to_watch: Corporate impairments; contractor receivables

channel: Interest rates (Sep 2026 +25 bp)
quantified: Observed margin response (net special commission income ÷ average assets): in the 2023 hiking year it rose at Riyad (2.93%→3.33%), SAB (2.52%→3.08%), ANB (2.78%→3.35%), BSF (2.87%→3.23%), Alinma (3.24%→3.50%) and SAIB (2.70%→2.86%), and fell at Al Rajhi (3.20%→2.71%), Bank Aljazira (2.38%→1.94%), Albilad (3.23%→3.01%) and SNB (2.83%→2.72%).
rationale: Banks with more floating-rate corporate lending gained from higher rates and lost margin in the 2024–25 cuts (SAIB 2.46%→2.14%). Banks with largely fixed-rate retail and Islamic financing behaved the other way. Al Rajhi's margin recovered as rates were cut, to 2.96% in FY2025 and 3.19% in 9M 2026. A single 25 bp rise is a small effect either way; SAMA follows the US Federal Reserve under the peg.
indicators_to_watch: SAMA decisions; 3M SAIBOR

channel: Household incomes, tariffs and retail credit
quantified: New residential mortgages: 2025 −12%, then stabilising in 2026 (Aug SAR 5.87bn, flat y/y).
rationale: Several confirmed measures support household income: SANED wage support, the Citizen Account extended to end-2027, the SAR 500 monthly allowance increase and higher Nitaqat wage floors (SAR 5,000 then 6,000). These support salary-based retail lending. The 2027 electricity and water tariffs raise household costs. Mortgage demand has stabilised after the 2025 fall. Retail-heavy banks are most exposed in both directions.
indicators_to_watch: Monthly mortgages; retail impairments

channel: Capital rules (countercyclical buffer)
quantified: 1% countercyclical buffer in effect since 25 May 2026 (measure confirmed).
rationale: The buffer must be met with common equity, so it is met mainly through retained earnings and lower payouts; Tier 1 sukuk do not count towards it. Banks' heavy AT1 issuance in 2026 (about SAR 34.5bn of sukuk, mostly AT1) raises Tier 1 ratios and funds growth. Its coupons reduce returns to ordinary shareholders, which our ROE already deducts.
indicators_to_watch: CET1 ratios; dividend payouts

channel: Corporate tax: Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax
direction: Negative for banks with low-taxed foreign entities
quantified: Not quantified: executive regulations pending.
rationale: Saudi banks pay mainly Zakat and some income tax at home. The top-up tax could apply to their foreign subsidiaries or branches where the effective tax rate is below 15%: SNB in Türkiye and Pakistan, Al Rajhi in Malaysia, Jordan and Kuwait, and others with foreign units. The effect depends on the regulations. No 2027 Zakat rule change was found (search to 26 Nov 2026).
indicators_to_watch: ZATCA regulations

rationale: Several banks report a significant escalation after 30 Sep 2026 as a subsequent event, and some have recorded management overlays. The budget's base case assumes recovery. If disruption persists, expect higher credit costs, especially for trade, contracting and SME exposures.
indicators_to_watch: Quarterly impairments; overlays
